bearings.paper_claim: On PANDORA DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 (+33.7% vs an IBM feature baseline of about 56.1) against best comparator AttRCNN 64.6. The authors say IBM moved away from LIWC toward open-vocabulary GloVe embeddings. In Table 7 the concept encoder adds about 2 pp AUC (68.0 with it vs 66.2 without). The paper does not rank closed-vocabulary scoring as a family.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 p. 209; Section 2 IBM statement (before p. 198); Table 7 and Section 4.4 pp. 211-212
bearings.system_side: Lexical Big Five in fec/members/big5_traits.py scores each member on closed-vocabulary LIWC/MRC-style per-1000-word category rates, standardizes them across the corpus, and combines them with standardized trait weights (published correlates, or a Mairesse SMOreg-style file when present).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is binary median-split self-report classification on Reddit, Facebook and student essays. The system is judged against RKH and Senate gold panels on congressional speech, which the paper never tests. The held-out CV figure of .350 vs RKH and the refit-to-RKH step were not located in the cited file, so they stay unverified.
bearings.verifier_note: Confirmed: 75.0, 64.6, +33.7%, IBM about 56.1, 68.0 vs 66.2, and the IBM LIWC statement. Not supported as written: closed-vocabulary scoring as the weakest family is the analyst's synthesis. The paper ranks IBM lowest but its feature rows include KNN 58.6 and XGBoost 58.9 on PANDORA. Reframed to the IBM-only claim.

bearings.paper_claim: On PANDORA BERT-Base reaches AUC 61.5, RoBERTa 63.2 and PersonaBERT 63.4, against DeepPerson 75.0. DeepPerson was pretrained on 800 million tokens vs 3.3 billion (BERT-Base) and 4.1 billion (PersonaBERT); RoBERTa used about 30 billion or more. The paper's ablation credits pseudo-labeling (SPDFiT) with about a 5-point AUC drop when removed.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 p. 209; Table 6 p. 210; Section 6 point 1 p. 218
bearings.system_side: fec/members/big5_llm.py header: item-level scoring with 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items (4 per trait), coarse -1/0/+1 responses, de-identified chunks of about 1,200 words sampled across each member's corpus, then averaged per member. The display-only status and the +0.064 behavioural-diagonal mean vs the .12 bar were not found in this file.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper compares fine-tuned encoder language models (the BERT family) on self-report labels, not zero-shot instruction-tuned LLM item readers. It bears on model size only indirectly, so it cannot confirm the Pink miss.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers confirmed (61.5, 63.2, 63.4, 75.0; 800M, 3.3B, 4.1B tokens; RoBERTa about 30B-plus). The claim that domain adaptation and pseudo-labeling drive the gap is interpretive: the ablation supports pseudo-labeling only. The system-side number could not be checked in the cited code.

bearings.paper_claim: The same GBDT and RFR models are run with and without personality features. Average MSE improvement: GBDT 14.29 percent (CH 20.91, SG&A 31.74, ROA 12.52), RFR 6.67 percent. GBDT gains from CNN-1 features 3.38, CNN-2 minus 1.80, BERT 8.62. Gains for all eight DVs are significant by Wilcoxon, GBDT at p below 0.01. Observations per DV range 405 to 519 (Table 10). A chronological split is reported in Online Appendix G.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 10-12 and Section 5 pp. 214-218; Online Appendix G (not in text file)
bearings.system_side: fec/members/behavioral_dispositions.py header: a label-free validation indicted the lexical Big Five for behavioural prediction (C reversed on participation, r_alerting -0.76), so dispositions are measured from behaviour. fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:58-64 defaults the basis to behavioral; the RECEPT_TRAITS environment variable reverts to lexical.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Borrow the design only: the same learner with and without a trait block, a held-out chronological split, and paired tests, applied to compare text traits against dispositions on a pre-registered responsiveness outcome. The lift magnitudes come from executives and firm accounting outcomes with reverse causality the authors leave unresolved, so they must not be quoted as evidence that text traits predict member behaviour.
bearings.verifier_note: All cited figures confirmed in Table 11 (RFR, average 6.67) and Table 12 (GBDT, average 14.29, CH 20.91, SG&A 31.74, ROA 12.52, CNN-1 3.38, CNN-2 minus 1.80, BERT 8.62). DV counts 405 to 519 confirmed in Table 10. Significance marks confirmed. Code header and default basis line match the claim; the code was read, not run.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors restrict their evaluation to social posts, forum messages and essays, and say speech transcripts and written articles may warrant exploration. The downstream case applies a model fine-tuned on Facebook labels to executives' tweets, and the text reports no executive-level survey validation.
bearings.system_side: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:65-73 defaults the N slot to affective (RECEPT_N environment variable). The cited fec/members/affective_n_validate.py:54-55 defines liwc_n, a lexical count-based N, and does not contain the rho .050 and .161 genre-transfer results.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:65-73; fec/members/affective_n_validate.py:54-55 (liwc_n definition only; transfer results not located in this file)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Support is for caution only. The paper runs no transfer test of its own, so it neither confirms nor explains the system's genre-transfer result.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper-side limitations confirmed. The code citation is wrong: lines 54-55 define a lexical N, not the affective N whose transfer results are claimed. Re-point to where the rho figures are computed, or drop the numbers.

bearings.paper_claim: Validity evidence is agreement with self-report surveys on non-elite authors. User-level Pearson correlations are at least 10 to 18 points above the best comparator and MSE at least 10 percent lower, reported in Online Appendix B and not in the body. No observer, expert or criterion validation is reported, and executive scores are used without survey validation.
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.2 p. 209; Section 5 p. 214; Online Appendix B (not in text file)
bearings.system_side: Gold-panel validation runs through fec/members/b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py (insider and academic panels) and fec/members/b5_gold_criterion_probes.py. The pass pattern in the analyst's summary (E and A on both panels, O and N on one, C on insider only) was not verified against any results file.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/big5_improvements_eval.py; fec/members/b5_residual_eval.py (paths corrected from fec root); fec/members/b5_gold_multitrait_validate.py
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's standard is self-report agreement on non-elite authors. It is weaker than and different in kind from the system's observer-panel standard, so its figures cannot substitute for a gold-panel look.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side confirmed: the 10-18 point and 10 percent MSE figures appear only in the body text pointing to Appendix B. The two code paths in the bearing were wrong (they are under fec/members/). The pass-pattern claim needs results files that were not read here.

Yang does not cite Ramey and does not test elite speech, so it neither contradicts nor confirms Ramey. Its feature-based rows rank lowest on non-elite self-report criteria. Item existence checked; Ramey content not read.
Thematic link only: Yang does not cite Koutsoumpis. Item existence checked; content not read, so the explanation of low LIWC-Big Five correlations is unverified.

summary_issues: Abstract says DeepPerson improves detection by 10-20 percentage points (text line 67); the body says 5-15 points vs best comparators (line 1817). Verified inconsistency.
Table 3 counts differ from the text: 3,000,068 posts vs 3,000,566 comments, and 9,917 updates vs 10,000. Verified.
Executive title counts (219 + 40 + 22 + 188 + 62 + 10 = 541) do not match the 352 executives. Verified inconsistency, also flagged by the analyst.

Summary and bearings say wlpHAN beats HAN, HCAN, SATT-LSTM, AttRCNN and Msg-Attn by 3-6 pp, which is the text claim (line near 2660). Table 7 gaps are about 9 to 12 pp for HAN, HCAN and SATT-LSTM (60.7, 61.1, 58.6 vs 70.3) and 5.7 pp for AttRCNN (64.6). Text and table disagree; cite table numbers.

SPDFiT is called the largest single contributor. Removing wlpHAN drops AUC about 5 pp (75.0 to 70.0) and replacing SPDFiT drops it to 64.7-65.2 (about 5 pp). The two effects are similar in size. The paper says SPDFiT matters in particular but does not rank it largest. Softened.
The ablation floor of 58.3 is Doc2Vec (setting 13, no pretraining), not an SPDFiT replacement. SPDFiT replacement settings 4-8 range 64.7-65.2.

The summary says the paper does not touch legislators. True of the body text, but the abstract cites a health case (pandemic infection rates) in an appendix that is not in the text file, and the summary omits it.

The summary calls closed-vocabulary scoring the weakest family. The paper ranks IBM lowest (AUC about 56.1) but makes no family-level claim, and its feature-based rows include KNN 58.6 and XGBoost 58.9 on PANDORA.

Bearing code paths are wrong: fec/big5_improvements_eval.py and fec/b5_residual_eval.py are under fec/members/. The affective_n_validate.py:54-55 citation points to liwc_n, not to the affective transfer results (rho .050, .161 not located).
Not located in the cited code: the .350 CV figure vs RKH, the refit-to-RKH step, the LLM display-only status and the +0.064 vs .12 figure. Treated as unverified.
Ramey relation changed from contradicts to complements: the paper does not cite Ramey or test elite speech, so it cannot contradict Ramey.
Related links to Koutsoumpis, Naz, Birkenmaier and Azucar are not cited in the paper text. Only item existence was checked, not their content. Pennebaker and King 1999 is cited (verified).
paul_alignment's 'dated but foundational' note for Ramey is not supported by the item: paul_entries is empty. Dropped, not verified.
Appendices A-I are not in the text file. Appendix B user-level tables, the essays results, Appendix G chronological split and Appendix H COVID case were not checked.

ARIMA is described as about 17% worse MSE than GBDT-DeepPerson. Text (near line 3460) says almost 17% worse; the Table 12 note calls the ARIMA row a relative improvement, which is ambiguous. Kept as the text states.

Verified as stated: GBDT MAE average 9.46 (text line 3789 and Table), average range 6.1-14.3 percent, 4-15 percent per variable, 800M tokens, 352 executives, 425 firms, 529 tweets per executive, 519 observations, 1.9 million essay words.
